Q. 
What is the purpose of the classification step of the ECOSS? 
1 
A. 
The Company’s transmission and distribution system is designed, operated, 
2 
and maintained to meet three primary objectives: 
3 
1. Connect customers to the distribution system; 
4 
2. Meet the peak requirements of each customer; and 
5 
3. Deliver power to customers. 
6 
Based on these objectives, each functionalized cost element is classified as 
7 
being one or more of customer-related, demand-related, or commodity-
8 
related, depending on which of the foregoing objectives it serves. 
9 
 
10 
Customer-related costs are incurred for assets that attach a customer to the 
11 
distribution system and to operate and maintain those assets, to meter the 
12 
customer’s usage, and to maintain customer accounts.  Customer-related 
13 
costs are primarily a function of the number of customers served, incurred 
14 
by the Company regardless of whether a particular customer uses any 
15 
electricity, and typically do not vary with usage or load profile.  Customer-
16 
related costs include capital and operating costs associated with the 
17 
customer portion of the primary and secondary distribution system, as well 
18 
as capital and operating costs for transformers, services, and meters.  They 
19 
also include the costs of metering, billing, customer service, and accounting 
20 
and collection activities.  Customer-related cost elements are allocated 
21 
Exhibit_____(E-RDP-1R) 
                       Schedule 2 
                           Rebuttal 
                   Page 664 of 696


--- Page 697 ---
among the classes based primarily on per-customer costs incurred (e.g., 
1 
services and meters) and on the number of customers served by a particular 
2 
activity. 
3 
 
4 
Demand, or capacity, related cost elements are associated with plant that is 
5 
designed, installed, and operated to meet peak customer demand.  Demand-
6 
related components include transmission system, the demand component of 
7 
distribution plant (including portions of poles, towers and fixtures, overhead 
8 
conductors, underground conduits and underground conductors), as well as 
9

considerations.

n. DEMAND AND CUSTOMER CLASSIFICATIONS
OF
DISTRIBUTION
PLANT ACCOUNTS
When the utility installs distribution plant to provide service to a customer and
to meet the individual customer's peak demand requirements, the utility must classify
distribution plant data separately into demand- and customer-related costs.
Classifying distribution plant as a demand cost assigns investment of that plant to
a customer or group of customers based upon its contribution to some total peak load.
The reason is that costs are incurred to serve area load, rather than a specific number of
customers.
Distribution substations costs (which include Accounts 360 -Land and Land
Rights, 361 - Structures and Improvements, and 362 -Station Equipment), are normally
classified as demand-related.
This classification is adopted because substations are nor-
mally built to serve a particular load and their size is not affected by the number of cus-
tomers to be served.
Distribution plant Accounts 364 through 370 involve demand and customer costs.
The customer component of distribution facilities is that portion of costs which varies
with the number of customers. Thus, the number of poles, conductors, transformers, serv-
ices, and meters are directly related to the number of customers on the utility's system.
As shown in Table 6-1, each primary plant account can be separately classified into a de-
mand and customer component.
Two methods are used to determine the demand and cus-
tomer components of distribution facilities. They are, the minimum-size-of-facilities
method, and the minimum-int~pt
cost (zero..intercept or positive-intercept cost, as ap-
plicable) of facilities.
A. The ft{inimum-Size Method
Classifying
distribution plant with the minimum-size method assumes that a
minimum size distribution system can be built to serve the minimum loading
requirements of the customer. The minimum-size method involves determining the
minimum size pole, conductor, cable, transformer, and service that is currently installed
by the utility. Normally, the average book cost for each piece of equipment determines
.

Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 18 of 77 
 
Each functionalized cost element is classified as being one or more of 
1 
customer-related, demand-related, or commodity-related, depending on 
2 
which of the foregoing objectives it serves. 
3 
 
4 
 
Costs that are incurred to connect a customer to the distribution system 
5 
and to operate and maintain those assets, to meter the customer’s usage, 
6 
and to maintain customer accounts, are classified as customer-related.  
7 
Customer-related cost elements are primarily a function of the number of 
8 
customers served and are incurred by the Company regardless of whether 
9 
an individual customer uses any gas.  Customer-related components 
10 
include capital and operating costs of the customer component of 
11 
distribution mains, and capital and operating costs of services, meters, and 
12 
house regulators.  They also encompass the costs of metering, billing, 
13 
customer service, and accounting and collection activities.  Customer-
14 
related cost elements are allocated among the classes based primarily on 
15 
number of customers. 
16 
 
17 
 
Cost elements that are associated with plant that is designed, installed, and 
18 
operated to meet peak hourly or daily customer gas requirements, are 
19 
classified as demand, or capacity, related.  Demand-related components 
20 
include transmission mains, the demand component of distribution mains, 
21 
Exhibit_____(E-RDP-1R) 
                       Schedule 2 
                           Rebuttal 
                   Page 677 of 696


--- Page 710 ---
Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 19 of 77 
as well as localized distribution facilities and dedicated facilities that are 
1 
designed to satisfy individual customer maximum demands.  Demand-
2 
related cost elements are allocated among the classes based on their 
3 
contributions to the peak daily demand for which the system is designed. 
4 
 
5 
Cost elements that generally vary with the volume of gas delivered (i.e., 
6 
throughput) to customers are classified as commodity-related. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Do all costs fit neatly into one of the classifications in the ECOSS – 
9 
demand, commodity, or customer? 
10 
A. 
Most assets and costs fit into one of the three classifications, but some 
11 
were split between demand and customer based on special studies as 
12 
shown in Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-3), Schedule 9, or based on the 
13 
classification of related assets or other related costs.  All assets and costs 
14 
in the Transmission function were classified as demand-related, and all 
15 
assets and costs in the Billing, Collections, and Sales Promotion functions 
16 
were classified as customer-related.  The costs in the Gas Supply and 
17 
Storage that are recovered in the MCG are classified as commodity-related 
18 
(the amount of costs recovered through the MCG was equal to MCG 
19 
revenue), and the balance of Gas Supply and Storage costs are classified 
20

Testimony of the Gas Rate Design Panel  
 
Page 20 of 77 
as demand-related.  Gas Procurement costs are classified as demand-
1 
related. 
2 
 
3 
Within the Distribution function, the costs related to services and meters 
4 
are classified as customer-related.  On the other hand, the costs related to 
5 
mains are classified to both demand and customer. 
6 
 
7 
Q. 
Please describe the process for determining how much of the 
8 
investment in distribution mains should be considered customer-
9 
related versus demand-related. 
10 
A. 
Distribution mains are installed to connect customers to the distribution 
11 
system (customer-related), as well as to provide capacity to meet customer 
12 
requirements on the design day (demand-related).  Therefore, the cost of 
13 
mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly demand-related.  
14 
The Company performed a minimum system study to determine the 
15 
customer-related portion of mains (Exhibit ___ (G-RDP-3), Schedule 9F).  
16 
Based on the results of the study, the customer component of mains was 
17 
computed to be 46.1 percent and the demand component 53.9 percent.  
18 
The customer component was allocated among the customer classes based 
19 
on the number of customers.  The demand component was allocated 
20 
among the customer classes based on their contribution to design-day 
21

B. Revenue Allocation 
1 
Q. 
Please summarize the methodology used to develop the Company’s 
2 
revenue allocation shown on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 1. 
3 
A.       The proposed revenue allocation is intended to move the revenue produced 
4 
by each service class closer to its revenue requirement as determined in the 
5 
ECOSS.   In developing the Company’s proposed revenue allocation, the 
6 
Panel considered the costs to provide the type and quality of service 
7 
required by each service class as determined in the ECOSS, while 
8 
mitigating extreme impacts on service classes, a widely-accepted concept 
9 
known as “gradualism.” 
10 
 
11 
A revenue increase, excluding gross revenue tax, of $99.292 million is 
12 
required to produce the target rate of return (Exhibit ___ (E-RRP-4, 
13 
Schedule 3, lines 27-29).  After reflecting changes in MFC and other 
14 
revenue, an increase in delivery rates of $102.269 million is needed (lines 
15 
30-37).  The amount to be recovered in Delivery rates is $1,683.2 million 
16 
(Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 3, line 19); the class revenue targets sum 
17 
to this amount (Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 1, line 37). 
18 
 
19 
The Company established a tolerance band, representing returns from 75 to 
20 
125 percent of the overall system return at current rates, equal to returns of 
21 
Exhibit_____(E-RDP-1R) 
                       Schedule 2 
                           Rebuttal 
                   Page 681 of 696


--- Page 714 ---
3.91 to 6.52 percent.  The use of the tolerance band allows the Company to 
1 
rely on the ECOSS results as a guide to allocating the increased revenue 
2 
requirement fairly, while also promoting the goal of gradualism.  The 
3 
Company determined whether each class was within the tolerance band and 
4 
under the average, within and close to the average, within and over the 
5 
average, above the band or well above the band. 
6 
 
7 
All classes were within the tolerance band, except for SC-1C – Residential 
8 
TOU, which was considerably above the band.  An increase in revenue of 
9 
2.00 percent is proposed for SC-1C.  All other classes are proposed to 
10 
increase by 6.2327 percent, the amount needed to produce the overall 
11 
revenue target.   
12 
 
13 
Q. 
What returns on rate base does the proposed revenue allocation 
14 
produce? 
15 
A. 
The proposed revenue allocation produces returns ranging from 4.7 percent 
16 
to 7.3 percent (except for SC1C, which is 14.8 percent) with the system 
17 
target return of 6.33 percent (line 46), and reflects the results of the ECOSS. 
18 
 
19 
Q. 
What rate classes are presented on Exhibit ___ (E-RDP-4), Schedule 1? 
20 
A.

Revenue Allocation 
The RD observed that both NFGD and Staff agree that 
the results of the Company’s Cost of Service study are best 
employed as a guide to evaluate class revenue levels and rate 
structures, but that other considerations are relevant before 
any final decisions are made.  As to revenue allocation, NFGD 
proposed an across the board average increase for each rate

class.  The RD concurred, rejecting both an MI proposal to 
increase the rates of the SC-1 and Cogeneration classes by 1.25 
times the system average, while allocating below average 
increases to the remaining commercial and industrial customers, 
and a UIU proposal based on its substitute ECOS study and 
methodology the crux of which would modify the results based on 
an allocation of NFGD’s mains as 100 percent demand related. 
UIU clarifies on exceptions that although it prefers 
the use of its methodology for calculating costs, insofar as its 
exceptions to the Company’s ECOS study are not adopted it 
supports the RD’s across-the-board revenue allocation.  MI, 
however, takes vigorous exception to the RD. 
MI breaks its exceptions down into four parts; that 
the RD’s revenue allocation conflicts with the cost-of-service 
evidence; is inequitable to SC 13 customers; is inconsistent 
with Commission precedent; and would establish an undesirable 
precedent.  MI’s exceptions are primarily grounded in its 
observation that NFGD’s ECOS study, adopted by the RD and 
earlier in this Order, demonstrates that certain classes, those 
admittedly containing MI’s constituents, are producing rates of 
return well in excess of the system average, while other 
classes, notably residential customers, are producing rates of 
return well below the system average.  MI advocates that the 
cost of service should be the primary criteria used to determine 
revenue allocation in this case.    
MI suggests that we should strive to move rates toward 
cost responsibility, especially in this case where the evidence 
shows that certain classes are producing rates of return more 
than double or even triple the system average.  To that end, MI 
argues that the ECOS study shows that several interclass 
subsidies exist.  Only by modifying the RD, claims MI, will we 
Exhibit_____(E-RDP-1R) 
                       Schedule 2 
                           Rebuttal 
                   Page 685 of 696

properly move revenue responsibility closer to the cost to 
serve. 
The only party that responded directly to MI in its 
brief opposing exceptions was UIU, with NFGD relying on its 
testimony and briefs as summarized in the RD.  UIU states that 
accepting MI’s proposal would result in the residential class 
being assigned revenue responsibility five times greater than 
the increases allocated to other service classes.  UIU notes 
that while it may be convenient to dilute revenue increases 
among the large proportional share of residential customers, 
such a result is unjust.  To the best we can discern, this seems 
to be the overarching concern shared by the ALJ in adopting 
NFGD’s across-the-board revenue allocation proposal, 
particularly in light of the public comments overwhelmingly 
provided by residential and low income customers.  However, as 
MI points out, and UIU admits by implication, there is some 
advantage to the residential class ability to dilute the 
increase, absorbing it across the largest populated class. 
UIU claims that, as a general matter, we should be 
skeptical of proposals to dilute rate increases by assigning 
them to the large residential customer classes.  We agree, and 
so confirm that the ability of the large residential class to 
absorb an increase is not what motivates our decision here.  
Rather, as MI notes, the cost of service study demonstrates that 
the rate of return disparities are significant, and it is 
consistent with sound ratemaking principles to correct them 
here.  Accordingly, we do accept MI’s exceptions and so modify 
the RD.

operations and maintenance expense project costs related to 
back-office system operating expenses, information technology 
discovery work, momentum services provided by the down-selected 
vendor, and legal costs associated with completing vendor 
contract negotiations.  The Company forecasted the three-month 
operations and maintenance expenses to be $3.335 million.  The 
Commission has traditionally applied a three-step process in 
examining requests for deferred accounting treatment.  To 
qualify for deferred accounting treatment, an item must be 
incremental to current rates; the amount must be material to the 
utility’s earnings and extraordinary in nature; and the utility 
cannot be overearning.  The AMI-related operations and 
maintenance expenses the Company is requesting to defer, for the 
three-month period, are incremental to current rates and the 
utility is not overearning.34  However, the forecasted level of 
incremental expenses for the three month period does not meet 
the Commission’s current policy on materiality.  The 
Commission’s current policy is that an item must exceed 5% of 
the company’s net income, available for common shareholders, to 
qualify for deferred accounting treatment.  However, the 
Commission has deviated from this standard for public policy 
reasons.  Given, the fact that the Company’s AMI proposal will 
directly benefit customers (i.e., provide customers with energy 
usage information that can be used to manage their costs, 
improve response times to power outages, enable the Company to 
assume the role of the DSP, and will facilitate customer access 
to third-party products and services to help conserve energy 
usage) and the BCA indicates the benefits of deploying AMI

3. Cost Allocation and Rate Design 
 
 
National Grid states that it generally uses the 
allocators from its Traditional Allocated Cost of Service Study 
provided during the consideration of its rate case filing in 
Cases 17-E-0238 and 17-G-0239.  To allocate certain costs,

                       Schedule 2

National Grid proposes to rely on cost-causation principles.  MI 
supports the Company’s cost allocation proposals.  As summarized 
above, MI also recommends a rate design for large non-
residential service classes.  UIU proposes that if the 
Commission approves the Company’s AMI proposal, rate design 
issues should be deferred to a future base rate proceeding.  
Pace proposes that AMI cost allocation should be more granularly 
functionalized to better reflect advanced functionalities of the 
AMI system than the traditional electric and gas meters.  Pace 
also proposes the Commission direct National Grid to develop a 
set of subaccounts and cost categories for tracking grid 
modernization-related investments. 
 
 
Only MI supports determining cost allocation and rate 
design at this time.  Furthermore, National Grid will only begin 
cost recovery after a rate order is issued in its currently 
pending rate proceedings, Cases 20-E-0380 and 20-G-381.  
Accordingly, it is reasonable to address these topics in the 
currently pending rate proceedings for National Grid to provide 
parties an opportunity to further refine the proposals and/or 
offer alternative allocation or rate design methods. 
 
Incentives and Metrics 
1. Incentives 
 
 
National Grid proposed that, if it were to deploy AMI 
as planned in the first six years, for at least $10 million 
below its forecasted capital costs, then its shareholders would 
retain 20% of the savings and customers would receive 80% of the 
savings.  UIU opposed this Capital Expenditure Efficiency 
Savings sharing mechanism.  The Commission agrees with UIU that 
this mechanism is not appropriate since deployment of AMI with 
lower capital expenditures than forecasted does not guarantee 
the expected level of benefits will materialize.  Indeed, 
Exhibit_____(E-RDP-1R) 
                       Schedule 2 
                           Rebuttal 
                   Page 692 of 696


--- Page 725 ---
decreased costs could result in decreased benefits.  National 
Grid has not proposed to guarantee any specific level of 
benefits with the forecasted or hypothetically reduced costs of 
the project.  Therefore, the Company’s proposed Capital 
Expenditure Efficiency Savings sharing mechanism is denied.  
Notwithstanding, the Commission reminds National Grid that it 
has a responsibility to control costs and make prudent 
investments.  Therefore, National Grid is expected to minimize 
the costs of this program even without the proposed mechanism. 
 
 
However, the Commission does support the concept of 
positive and/or negative incentives related to the AMI project.  
This topic should be considered holistically in the context of 
base rate proceedings, such as in the Company’s rebuttal/update 
testimony to be filed in Cases 20-E-0380 and 20-G-0381, or in 
future rate proceedings.  The Company may propose positive 
incentives if the Company creates increased net benefits to 
customers through actions such as, but not limited to, 
significant advancement of the deployment schedule, 
identification and implementation of additional features that 
significantly increase customer benefits, or significant 
advancement of customer benefits already identified while 
controlling overall capital and O&M costs.  Negative incentives 
may be considered to account for circumstances where National 
Grid fails to produce promised outcomes key to the 
implementation and success of the AMI project.  In addition, 
Mission:Data’s proposal to link cost recovery to the realization 
of customer benefits can also be considered.  The amount of the 
positive and/or negative incentives shall be derived by 
accounting for the financial impact the actions being 
incentivized will have on customers.

consideration by the Commission, AMI-related PSRs for potential
